Keep explosive chemicals away from heat, flames, sparks, friction and shock. Handle and store them carefully and follow the instructions.
Reactive chemicals can react violently, causing fires or explosions, releasing harmful gases, and damaging skin, eyes or property.
Limit the time exposed to radiation and maximize distance from its source; use suitable shielding.
Asphyxiant chemicals, such as gases that displace oxygen, can cause suffocation.
Signs and symbols warn of hazards and explain how to handle and store chemicals safely, helping prevent accidents.
Raise the alarm and inform the teacher or lab incharge. Use the appropriate firefighting method only if safe; otherwise evacuate and follow emergency instructions.
Drills help people learn how to respond quickly and calmly, reducing confusion and injuries during a real emergency.
Raise the alarm and alert the teacher or lab incharge. Switch off the electricity only if safe, do not use water on the electrical fire, and evacuate by a safe route.
Carry out reactions that produce toxic, irritating or otherwise harmful gases and vapours in a fume cupboard.
Follow laboratory instructions and wear suitable protective equipment. Keep chemicals labelled and learn the emergency procedures.
Radiation is shown by the radiation trefoil. An asphyxiant warning indicates a substance that can cause suffocation, often by displacing oxygen.
An impact can trigger a rapid reaction in unstable, shock-sensitive chemicals. The reaction releases heat and gases, which may cause an explosion.

Explosive chemicals can detonate due to heat, flames, sparks, friction or shock, causing blast injuries, burns and damage. Toxic chemicals can poison through inhalation, swallowing or skin contact; toxic gases can cause serious illness or death.

Read labels and follow instructions; wear suitable protective equipment; never taste chemicals or allow direct contact; keep the laboratory tidy and store chemicals properly; report accidents and know emergency procedures.

Warning signs and symbols identify hazards such as corrosive, toxic, explosive, radiation and asphyxiant dangers. They help people take suitable precautions and handle and store chemicals safely, preventing accidents.
Examples include potassium cyanide, chlorine and phenol. A toxic gas can be inhaled and cause poisoning, breathing difficulty, serious illness or death.

Warn others and alert the teacher or lab incharge. Keep people away and do not touch or clean the spill yourself. Remove ignition sources only if safe, follow the chemical's emergency instructions, and evacuate if necessary. Have trained personnel manage the spill using appropriate equipment.

Inspect and maintain tankers, containers and valves; use approved, leak-proof equipment and secure loads; train handlers; follow transport regulations and safe routes; use leak detectors and emergency plans, including prompt public warnings and evacuation procedures.
